title: The Snow Giant of the Himalayas

pages.text: In Madam Lomotey’s classroom, the world map showed a long wrinkle of white on the far side of the world: the Himalayas, the tallest mountains on Earth. “Today’s mystery,” she said, “is a creature that people there have talked about for a long time. They call it the yeti, or snow giant.”
sentences: In Madam Lomotey’s classroom, the world map showed a long wrinkle of white on the far side of the world: the Himalayas, the tallest mountains on Earth.
“Today’s mystery,” she said, “is a creature that people there have talked about for a long time.
They call it the yeti, or snow giant.”
pages.alt: A teacher points to the Himalayas on a world map in a Ghanaian classroom.

pages.text: “Tall, hairy, walks on two legs,” said Rashid, reading a card. “Some people say they have seen huge footprints in the snow. Some say they have seen a giant shape far away.” Selinam raised her hand. “But has anyone caught one?” “No,” said Madam Lomotey. “That is why it is a mystery.”

Some say they have seen a giant shape far away.” Selinam raised her hand.

pages.alt: Children read a card about the yeti while one raises her hand.

pages.text: “A mystery needs more than a story,” said Madam Lomotey. “It needs a question we can test.” Selinam wrote three questions: What did people see? What evidence is there, like hair, bones or footprints? And what could the evidence be?
sentences: “A mystery needs more than a story,” said Madam Lomotey.
“It needs a question we can test.” Selinam wrote three questions: What did people see?
What evidence is there, like hair, bones or footprints?
And what could the evidence be?
pages.alt: A girl writes three questions on the board.

pages.text: “Scientists did test the evidence,” said Madam. “In 2017, a team led by Dr Charlotte Lindqvist studied hair, teeth, bone and other samples from the Himalayas that people said were from yetis. Nine of them came from museums and private collections.” “And?” asked Rashid. “And,” said Madam, “they used DNA, a code inside every living thing.”
sentences: “Scientists did test the evidence,” said Madam.
“In 2017, a team led by Dr Charlotte Lindqvist studied hair, teeth, bone and other samples from the Himalayas that people said were from yetis.
Nine of them came from museums and private collections.” “And?” asked Rashid.
“And,” said Madam, “they used DNA, a code inside every living thing.”
pages.alt: A scientist looks at a hair sample under a microscope.

pages.text: “What was the result?” “Nearly all the samples came from bears: Himalayan brown bears, Tibetan brown bears and one Asian black bear. One sample came from a dog.” Rashid’s eyes went wide. “So the snow giant was a bear?” “Those samples were,” said Madam. “That is a real answer.”
sentences: “What was the result?” “Nearly all the samples came from bears: Himalayan brown bears, Tibetan brown bears and one Asian black bear.
One sample came from a dog.” Rashid’s eyes went wide.
“So the snow giant was a bear?” “Those samples were,” said Madam.
“That is a real answer.”
pages.alt: A shaggy brown bear stands in snow beside a scientist’s chart.

pages.text: “But does it solve everything?” asked Selinam. “Think like a scientist,” said Madam. “The study tested those samples. It did not search every mountain for ever. And it can explain why people may have mistaken bears for giants: bears can stand on two legs and leave big prints. But it cannot tell us what every person saw.”

“Think like a scientist,” said Madam.
“The study tested those samples.
It did not search every mountain for ever.
And it can explain why people may have mistaken bears for giants: bears can stand on two legs and leave big prints.
But it cannot tell us what every person saw.”
pages.alt: Children think with thought bubbles showing a bear standing and big footprints.

pages.text: “So why do people still tell the story?” asked Rashid. Madam smiled. “Stories are about more than evidence. In the high mountains, people have told yeti stories for generations, and for some they carry feelings about the mountains: huge, wild and not fully known. A good scientist respects a story and still asks for proof.”

In the high mountains, people have told yeti stories for generations, and for some they carry feelings about the mountains: huge, wild and not fully known.
A good scientist respects a story and still asks for proof.”
pages.alt: Elders and children sit around a fire while a teacher listens.

pages.text: At the end, the class made two lists. Solved: the tested samples came from bears. Not solved: what some people saw, and whether any unknown animal lives there. “We do not have to pretend,” said Selinam. “We can write: we do not know yet.” Madam Lomotey nodded. “That,” she said, “is the best answer a scientist can give.” The end.

activities.question: What did the DNA study find about the tested “yeti” samples?
options: They came from a giant ape
They came from a mountain goat

activities.prompt: Scientists have hair, teeth and bone samples. What could DNA tell them about the animal?
options: Which kind of animal each sample came from
The animal’s name in a local language

activities.question: Why does the DNA result not solve every part of the mystery?
options: It tested only some samples and cannot explain what every person saw
Bears do not live in the Himalayas

activities.definition: Facts or objects that help show whether something is true.

items: People told stories of a snow giant.
Scientists collected hair and other samples.
DNA tests showed nearly all were from bears.
The class listed what was solved and not solved.

activities.prompt: Selinam said “we do not know yet.” How does it feel to say that when you are not sure?

glossary.definition: A tall, hairy creature in stories from the Himalayan mountains.
A code inside living things that tells what kind of living thing they are.
Facts or objects that help show what is true.
Something that is not yet explained.
